readerTitle: Build, buy or partner: why the cheaper option on paper can cost more
caseNote: 가상 사례 (유통회사 운영팀의 배송 경로 소프트웨어, 철물점 체인의 당일 배송) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 새 역량을 만들지, 사을지, 제휴할지는 가격표가 아니라 '기다리는 동안 잃는 돈'과 '그 역량이 고객이 우리를 고르는 이유인가'로 판단한다.
misconception: 직접 만들면 한 번만 돈을 내니 매년 돈을 내는 구매나 제휴보다 싸다.

sources.text: Capron, L. & Mitchell, W. (2012). Build, Borrow, or Buy: Solving the Growth Dilemma. Harvard Business Review Press.
경영 전략의 표준 개념 (make-or-buy 결정, 기회비용)

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 가격표 비교: 직접 개발 $120,000 vs 구매 $5,000 × 36개월 = $180,000, 차이 $60,000.
Capron & Mitchell(2012)의 서지 정보(출판사, 연도)를 게시 전에 확인하세요. 카드 본문에서는 인용하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Building it yourself looks $60,000 cheaper.
body: An operations team at a distribution company needs route-planning software. The company's IT group can build it for $120,000. A vendor rents a ready-made tool for $60,000 a year.
Over three years, building looks like the bargain. Run the full numbers and it costs almost twice as much.

image.label: Two price tags: one small, one big, with a calendar behind the small one
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에 작은 가격표 "$120,000 Build", 오른쪽에 큰 가격표 "$180,000 Buy". 작은 가격표 뒤에 9장이 넘어가는 달력이 그림자처럼 길게 늘어져 있음. 실제 소프트웨어 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Build or buy the routing tool?
body: You lead the operations team. The tool should save about $20,000 a month in fuel and overtime.
**Build:** $120,000, ready in 9 months, then about $2,500 a month to maintain. **Buy:** $5,000 a month, live in 1 month. Over three years, which costs less?

options.feedback: You compared price tags only. That misses the upkeep and the nine months of savings you don't get while you wait.

options.text: Buy. Going live 8 months sooner is worth more than the price gap
options.feedback: Right. Every month without the tool costs $20,000 in savings you never see. Speed is the biggest number here.

options.text: They're close, so build for the extra control
options.feedback: Control has real value, and sometimes it's worth paying for. But here the gap isn't close. The next card shows how wide it is.

cards.title: The price tag is the smallest part.
body: **Build:** $120,000 + $67,500 upkeep (27 months) + $180,000 in missed savings (9 months) = **$367,500**.
**Buy:** $180,000 + $20,000 in missed savings (1 month) = $200,000. Buying wins by $167,500.

cards.title: Build, buy or partner
body: When you need a capability you don't have, there are three ways to get it. **Build** it yourself: most control, but slowest, and you carry the upkeep. **Buy** it, as a product or even a whole company: fastest, but you pay up front or forever.
**Partner** with someone who already has it: quick and cheaper, but you depend on them and share the reward.

image.label: Three paths to the same goal: a toolbox, a shopping bag, a handshake
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽에 "Need: new capability", 오른쪽으로 세 갈래 길. 공구상자 "Build: control, slow", 쇼핑백 "Buy: fast, costly", 악수 "Partner: shared, dependent". 실제 기업 로고 없음.

cards.title: Two questions decide most cases.
body: Price tags rarely settle it. Ask these instead:
list: **Is this why customers choose us?** If yes, control matters, so lean toward building.
**What does each month of waiting cost?** If a lot, lean toward buying or partnering.
**Do we need something we can't easily own,** like someone else's customers, network or licenses? Then partner.
cards.callout: Build what makes you different. Buy or borrow the rest.

cards.title: When the expensive option is the right one.
body: Now imagine the company wins contracts because its trucks arrive in tighter time windows than any rival's. Routing isn't support work anymore. It's the reason customers sign.
A rented tool your rivals can rent too won't keep you ahead. The $167,500 gap might be the price of an edge nobody can copy.
cards.softwareNote: Software founders face this daily. Few build their own payments or login systems. They rent them and spend scarce engineers on the features customers actually pay for.

cards.title: Each path hides a cost.
body: Build estimates often run late, and here every extra month costs $20,000. Buying a whole company is harder than buying software: people, systems and habits have to be merged, and that can take years.
Partners can raise prices, get bought or lose interest. Some learn your business well enough to compete with you. Before partnering, decide what you'd do if they walked away.

cards.title: Now it's a hardware store chain.
body: You run 12 hardware stores. Customers keep asking for same-day delivery. You don't know how many orders you'd get, and delivery isn't what you're known for. Your edge is expert staff and stock.

options.text: Partner with a local delivery service, paid per order
options.feedback: You're live in weeks and pay only when orders come in. You give up some control and margin, but you learn real demand before committing.

options.text: Buy a small local courier business
options.feedback: You'd get drivers and control fast. But you'd take on a whole company and its costs before knowing if customers will order enough.

options.text: Build your own fleet: 10 vans and drivers for all stores
options.feedback: Full control, but slow and costly up front. You'd be paying vans and wages for demand you haven't seen yet, for something that isn't your edge.

cards.title: Build what makes you different. Buy or partner for the rest.
body: Count what waiting costs, not just the price tag, and ask whether the capability is why customers pick you.
**Try it today:** pick one project you plan to do in-house. Write down how many months it will take and what each month without it costs.
